title: A pact
hook: whoever finds the deathless first will tell the other

segments.voice: Yesterday: Upatissa and Kolita, gone quiet at the festival, and your line, the show was empty. Today the two friends set out.

Two hikers reach a fork in a trail at dusk and agree to split up. Whoever finds the way down first comes back for the other. It's a simple deal, and it only works if both of them would really come back. Upatissa and Kolita make a deal like that, not about a trail, but about the deepest thing they can name. They've left the festival and their families' comforts to live as wanderers. And along the way they make each other a promise that will shape the rest of their lives.
screen: `A FORK IN THE TRAIL.` → `WHOEVER FINDS IT, COMES BACK.` → `THE TWO FRIENDS PROMISE.`

segments.voice: First, the teacher. In Rajagaha lives a wandering teacher named Sanjaya, with a large following of wanderers. The two friends go forth under him. The commentaries say they quickly learned everything he had to teach, and then asked: is there more? There wasn't. In another discourse, Sanjaya is remembered for answers that slip away when you reach for them: asked a hard question, he would say neither yes, nor no, nor neither. For these two, that was not a place to stop. Second, the word. What were they looking for? The Vinaya uses one word for it: the deathless. In Pali, amata. Not long life. Not a heaven that might end. The deathless names freedom from the whole round of birth and death, the thing the festival couldn't give. Third, the pact. As the Vinaya tells it, the two had given their word to each other: whoever reaches the deathless first will tell the other. No conditions. No race. No prize for winning. Just: if I get there, you'll hear of it. Fourth, why it matters. A seeker could easily turn inward and forget everyone else. These two built friendship into the search itself; each one's freedom was tied to the other's. And the pact assumes something: that one of them might get there without the other, and that whoever did would not be too proud, too busy or too far gone to come back. Tomorrow, one of them finds something.
screen: `A TEACHER WITH NO MORE TO GIVE.` · `AMATA: THE DEATHLESS.` · `WHOEVER FINDS IT FIRST WILL TELL.` · `FRIENDSHIP BUILT INTO THE SEARCH.` · then, large: `WHOEVER FINDS IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Bring a friend to mind, someone whose good you want, and think of one small, honest promise you could keep for them: not a grand vow, just something true. Hold it, picture keeping it, and rest with the breath.
A pact. Two friends, wanderers under Sanjaya, promise each other: whoever finds the deathless first will tell the other. Today's word.
Your line: whoever finds it first. Friendship, built into the search itself. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhist teaching gives great weight to good friendship; in the discourses the Buddha calls admirable friendship the whole of the holy life (SN 45.2), and in some communities monks and lay people practice in small groups who support each other.

To stay with their teacher Sanjaya forever, whatever happened.

chat.meaning: The Vinaya says they gave their word: whoever reaches the deathless first will tell the other. No race, no prize.

amata.meaning: the deathless, freedom from the round of birth and death

notes: All material paraphrased. Rhys Davids and Oldenberg translated the Mahavagga (SBE 13), but the writer was not certain of the exact wording of the pact, so it is not quoted.

Confirm Mahavagga 1.23: Sanjaya living at Rajagaha with a large company of wanderers; Sariputta and Moggallana living the holy life under him; their agreement that whoever first attained the deathless (amata) would tell the other.
DN 2: confirm Sanjaya's 'eel-wriggling' reply pattern (not saying it is so, not otherwise, not neither). The script uses it only as a description of Sanjaya in that discourse.
Commentary detail that they quickly learned all Sanjaya had and asked if there was more; confirm.
Hook: the friends 'left their families' comforts' summarizes their going forth; the script does not use the commentary's numbers of followers.
howItsDone cites SN 45.2 (Ananda calls good friendship half the holy life; the Buddha says the whole); paraphrased.
